RELIGIOUS CONFLICT

OPENING QUOTE: CARDINAL BASIL HUME
- "Many people need enemies for their own sense of identity." They are defined as much by what they oppose as by what they support.
- Conflict and confrontation mark much of our politics, industrial relations and international affairs.
- It is often easier to mobilise people to oppose than to co-operate. Hostility, anger and envy grow.
- But those who see themselves as children of God and part of a single creation must reject these attitudes.
- They develop "partnership not conflict, friendship not hostility, peace not war."

KEY TERMS (ONE-LINE DEFINITIONS)
- Intolerance: refusing to accept or respect people of other beliefs.
- Prejudice: judging others negatively in advance, without good reason (e.g. because of their religion).
- The Golden Rule: the teaching, found in almost all religions, that you should treat others as you would like to be treated.
- Religion and conflict: the question of how far religion causes, or is used in, conflicts between groups.
- Exclusive revelation: a religion's claim that it alone knows God's will.
- Denomination: a branch within one religion (Christianity has some 20,000).
- PLO: Palestine Liberation Organisation.
- NICRA: Northern Ireland Civil Rights Association, formed 1967.
- Decommissioning: putting weapons beyond use.
- Direct rule: Northern Ireland governed directly from Westminster (London), from 1972.

GROUP WORK HEADLINE
- "John Paul becomes first Pope to visit a mosque" (Irish Times headline, 1 May 2001).
- Despite brave efforts by church leaders, religious conflict continues in many parts of the world.

CAUSES OF RELIGIOUS CONFLICT
- From early times, intolerance, prejudice and competition between religions - and even between denominations within the same "parent" religion - have led to inter-religious strife and conflict.
- Christianity has some 20,000 different denominations.
- Some religions claim an EXCLUSIVE revelation of God's will.
- Together with an endless variety in ritual practice and interpretation of doctrine, this leads to suspicion, misunderstandings and even oppression.

POPE JOHN PAUL II AT ASSISI (1986)
- He prayed in Assisi in 1986 with Jews, Muslims, Hindus and Buddhists.
- He said our relationships with God and with others depend so much on each other that Scripture says: "He who does not love, does not know God" (1 John 4:8).

CATHOLIC TEACHING: NOSTRA AETATE PARAGRAPH 5
- There is no basis, in theory or practice, for discrimination between individuals or peoples, because of human dignity and the rights that flow from it.
- The Church condemns, "as foreign to the mind of Christ, any discrimination against people or any harassment of them on the basis of their race, colour, condition in life or religion".
- This is the Catholic ideal, but the lived experience of many Christians does not reflect Christ's message to love one's neighbour.

THE GOLDEN RULE IN SEVEN RELIGIONS (LEARN THESE)
- HINDUISM (Mahabharata 5:1517): "This is the sum of duty: Do nothing unto others which would cause you pain if it were done to you."
- BUDDHISM (Udana-Varga 5:18): "Hurt not others in ways you yourself would find hurtful."
- CONFUCIANISM (Analects of Confucius 15:23): "Do not unto others what you would not have them do unto you."
- JUDAISM (Talmud, Shabbat 31a): "What is hateful to you, do not do to your fellow human being. That is the law; all the rest is commentary."
- CHRISTIANITY (Matthew 7:12): "Always treat others as you would like them to treat you: that is the Law and the Prophets."
- ISLAM (Sunna): "No one of you is a believer until he desires for his brother that which he desires for himself."
- SIKHISM (Guru Granth Sahib 259): "Do not create enmity with anyone, for God is within everyone."

WHY THE GOLDEN RULE IS IGNORED
- It is ignored when political or social ideologies and aims cloud, or completely overshadow, the true religious and ethical teachings of a faith.
- This leads to prejudice, oppression, hatred, exclusion and violence.

KAREN ARMSTRONG
- The external history of a religion often seems divorced from the real purpose (raison d'etre) of faith.
- The spiritual quest is an INTERIOR journey - "a psychic rather than a political drama" - concerned with liturgy, doctrine, contemplative disciplines and the exploration of the heart, not with the clash of current events.
- Religions do have a life outside the soul: leaders deal with the state and world affairs and often enjoy doing so.
- They fight members of other faiths who seem to challenge their claim to "a monopoly of absolute truth", and persecute their own co-religionists for interpreting the tradition differently or holding heterodox (unorthodox) beliefs.
- Priests, rabbis, imams and shamans are often as consumed by worldly ambition as ordinary politicians.
- But this is generally seen as an ABUSE of a sacred ideal. Power struggles are not what religion is really about, but "an unworthy distraction from the life of the spirit", which is unseen, silent and unobtrusive.
- In many faiths monks and mystics lock themselves away, as the clamour and strife of history is seen as incompatible with a truly religious life.

PAOLO DALL'OGLIO AND DEIR MAR MUSA
- Paolo Dall'Oglio is an Italian Jesuit priest.
- He founded a Christian community high on a cliff in the Syrian desert called "Deir Mar Musa", the Community of St Moses the Ethiopian.
- The community prays, works and offers hospitality to all.
- Aim: encourage positive relationships between Muslims and Christians in a spirit of respect, love and reconciliation.
- His words: "everyone knows that we cannot continue to use religion as an excuse for violence of all kinds. We have to find a way to break through the infernal circle of fear that we feel, all of us."
- The chapter says his words are a challenge for all people of faith in the twenty-first century.

CONFLICT 1: ISRAEL AND THE PALESTINIANS - BACKGROUND
- 135 CE: the Romans drove the Jews out of Jerusalem and named the area Palaestina (Palestine).
- The Jews fled to the northernmost part; the main territory was occupied by Christian converts.
- Muslim Arab armies moved north from Arabia and conquered most of the Middle East, including Palestine (the textbook dates this to the sixth century).
- Muslims stayed in control until the early twentieth century. Jews and Christians were mostly allowed to practise their religion.
- Jerusalem became a holy city for Muslims because, according to the Qur'an, Muhammad ascended to heaven from there.
- The Al Aqsa Mosque was built to mark the site, on an area generally regarded as the place of the old Jewish Temple. (Picture: the Al Aqsa Mosque and the Western (Wailing) Wall in Jerusalem.)
- After World War II: the United Nations recommended dividing Palestine into an Arab state and a Jewish state, with international administration of Jerusalem. This did not work and hostility broke out between the Arab League and the Jews.
- 1948: the Jews proclaimed Israel an independent state. War continued on and off until 1949.
- 1949: an uneasy truce began, lasting until the 1960s.
- The PLO (Palestine Liberation Organisation) was formed then, with support from neighbouring Arab leaders, to carry out military action against Israel.
- Israel retaliated strongly against neighbouring Arab states; the Israeli-Arab war has continued to the present day.

PEACE ATTEMPTS
- The Camp David Agreement between Israel and Egypt.
- The Oslo Declaration and Agreement between Israel and the PLO.
- As a result of the peace process, Israel withdrew from the Gaza Strip and the West Bank.
- Palestinians set up a government under Yassar Arafat.
- Violence has continued on and off despite a United States pledge to re-launch the peace process.

ROLE OF RELIGION IN THE ISRAELI-PALESTINIAN CONFLICT
- Not an easy question, even though it involves Palestinian Muslims and Israeli Jews.
- For both Jews and Muslims, religious identity carries political and cultural undertones.
- For many, religious identity is inextricably (inseparably) linked with ideas of homeland and claims over territory.
- PHILIP BARNES (World Religions): it depends on what one means by religion.
- For the Palestinians it is a religious conflict, but only in an extended sense of religion, one that "subsumes politics under religion" (politics is included within religion).
- For the Jews, the religious sense is even weaker ("more attenuated"): they simply want a homeland where they will find security and peace, a hope that has escaped them for most of their history.

CONFLICT 2: NORTHERN IRELAND - BACKGROUND
- 1921: partition of Ireland (also in chapter 1).
- Mostly Protestant unionists in the Six Counties wanted to keep ties with Britain.
- Mostly Catholic nationalists wanted to join the Republic and form a thirty-two county state.
- On the surface religion seems central to the conflict.
- During the twentieth century attitudes hardened on both sides with IRA campaigns and the predictable loyalist backlash.
- The Protestant majority in the North moved to secure its domination through legislation and other means. This discrimination fuelled nationalist and republican fervour.
- 1967: the Northern Ireland Civil Rights Association (NICRA) was formed to campaign for the removal of discrimination, modelled on the civil rights campaign in the United States.
- The local administration could not deal with the growing disorder, and British troops were sent in to restore order. (The textbook prints the year as 1965, which appears to be a misprint since it comes after NICRA in 1967 in the story.)
- The troops' arrival further inflamed republicanism. Soon after, the Provisional IRA was formed and began a campaign of violence against the army.
- 1972: direct rule from Westminster imposed. This began what is "euphemistically" called "The Troubles".
- Between 1974 and the 1994 ceasefires there were seven attempts to reach a settlement.
- Good Friday 1998: the Belfast Agreement was signed by political representatives of both traditions.
- The peace process continues; ceasefires hold; the British and Irish governments keep working to get both traditions to share power.
- September 2005: General John de Chastelain, Chairman of the Independent International Commission on Decommissioning, declared that the IRA had decommissioned all its arsenal (weapons).
- It remained to be seen whether this would persuade unionists to share power with nationalists.

ROLE OF RELIGION IN THE NORTHERN IRELAND CONFLICT
- On the surface, Catholics = republican side, Protestants = unionist side.
- But it can be argued it is mainly a struggle for ECONOMIC and POLITICAL domination between two opposing groups.
- Centuries of British domination and struggles for Irish independence have shaped attitudes.
- Question: how far are people in modern secular Ireland really committed to their religious beliefs?
- The irony of two groups of Christians waging war on each other has often been pointed out.
- PHILIP BARNES: if religion is related to politics in a more self-critical way that challenges existing alliances between religion and Northern Irish politics, "then the conflict may not be religious at all" (or religious only in a sense different from authentic Christian belief and practice).

GANDHI (FROM THE ASSIGNMENTS)
- Mahatma Gandhi, the great Hindu holy man and leader: "The terrible crimes of history are the fault, not of religion, but of the ungovernable brute in human beings."

FRAMEWORK FOR STUDYING A RELIGIOUS CONFLICT (FROM THE ASSIGNMENTS)
- Give a historical overview.
- Examine the position of citizens and groups in terms of political, religious and financial freedom and opportunity.
- Comment on how political leaders use religion to further their own goals.
- Explain how misinterpretation of religious beliefs and values fuels hostility of ordinary followers towards the other group.
- Suggest ways the groups can reconcile and build a better society.

CHAPTER KEY TERMS LIST
- Intolerance, Prejudice, The Golden Rule, Religion and conflict.

rows.prompt: Why was NICRA formed in 1967 and what followed?
rows.model_answer: NICRA was formed to campaign for the removal of discrimination against nationalists, modelled on the US civil rights campaign. rows.prompt: Explain why some argue that the Northern Ireland conflict is not mainly religious.
rows.model_answer: Although Catholics are linked with republicans and Protestants with unionists, it can be argued it is mainly a struggle for economic and political domination, shaped by centuries of British rule and the fight for independence. Many people in secular Ireland may not be deeply committed to their beliefs, and the irony of Christians fighting Christians has often been noted.

rows.prompt: Examine the role of religious belief in the conflict between Israel and the Palestinians.
rows.model_answer: The conflict has deep roots. In 135 CE the Romans drove the Jews out of Jerusalem and named the area Palaestina. Muslim Arab armies later conquered the region and stayed in control until the early twentieth century, mostly allowing Jews and Christians to practise their faith. Jerusalem became holy to Muslims because, according to the Qur'an, Muhammad ascended to heaven there, and the Al Aqsa Mosque was built on the area regarded as the site of the old Jewish Temple. After World War II the UN plan to divide Palestine failed, and in 1948 the Jews proclaimed Israel an independent state. War followed, the PLO was formed to take military action, and Israel retaliated strongly. Peace efforts such as Camp David and the Oslo Agreement led to Israeli withdrawal from Gaza and the West Bank and a Palestinian government under Yassar Arafat, yet violence continued. Religion's role is complex because for both Jews and Muslims religious identity carries political and cultural undertones and is linked to homeland and territory. Philip Barnes argues that for Palestinians it is religious only in an extended sense that 'subsumes politics under religion', while for Jews it is even less religious: they simply want a secure, peaceful homeland. So religion shapes identity, but land and security drive the conflict.

rows.prompt: 'The conflict in Northern Ireland is a religious conflict.' Discuss.
rows.model_answer: On the surface, religion seems central. After partition in 1921, mostly Protestant unionists in the Six Counties wanted to keep ties with Britain, while mostly Catholic nationalists wanted to join a thirty-two county state. Attitudes hardened with IRA campaigns and the loyalist backlash. The Protestant majority secured its domination through legislation and other means, and this discrimination fuelled nationalist fervour. In 1967 NICRA campaigned for civil rights; disorder grew, British troops arrived, the Provisional IRA began its campaign and direct rule was imposed in 1972, starting 'The Troubles'. After seven attempts at settlement and the 1994 ceasefires, the Belfast Agreement was signed on Good Friday 1998, and in 2005 General John de Chastelain confirmed IRA decommissioning. However, it can be argued the conflict is mainly a struggle for economic and political domination between two groups, shaped by centuries of British domination and struggles for independence. In modern secular Ireland it is questionable how committed people really are to their religious beliefs, and the irony of Christians waging war on each other has often been noted. Philip Barnes suggests that if religion related to politics more self-critically, the conflict 'may not be religious at all', or religious only in a sense distinct from authentic Christianity. So religion marks identity, but politics and power are the main causes.
rows.marking_scheme: Very good 16-20, good 10-15, fair 0-9. May refer to: partition 1921; unionist/nationalist and Protestant/Catholic identity; discrimination; NICRA 1967; troops; Provisional IRA; direct rule 1972; Troubles; ceasefires 1994; Good Friday 1998; decommissioning 2005; economic/political domination argument; secular Ireland; irony of Christians fighting; Barnes quote. Must weigh both sides.

rows.prompt: What is the Golden Rule? Explain how it is expressed in three world religions and why it is often ignored.
rows.model_answer: The Golden Rule is a central teaching, found in almost every religion, that we should treat others as we would want to be treated ourselves. In Christianity Jesus says, 'Always treat others as you would like them to treat you: that is the Law and the Prophets' (Matthew 7:12). In Judaism the Talmud teaches, 'What is hateful to you, do not do to your fellow human being. That is the law; all the rest is commentary' (Shabbat 31a). In Islam the Sunna says, 'No one of you is a believer until he desires for his brother that which he desires for himself.' Hinduism, Buddhism, Confucianism and Sikhism have similar teachings; Sikhism adds, 'Do not create enmity with anyone, for God is within everyone.' Yet the Golden Rule is often ignored. When political or social ideologies cloud or overshadow the true religious and ethical teachings of a faith, the result is prejudice, oppression, hatred, exclusion and violence. Karen Armstrong notes that religious leaders may be as consumed by worldly ambition as politicians, fighting others who challenge their claim to absolute truth. The Catholic Church condemns discrimination as 'foreign to the mind of Christ', but the lived experience of many Christians does not match this ideal.
rows.marking_scheme: Definition: 2 marks. Three religions: 3 x 3 marks (religion named + accurate wording/source). Why ignored: 9 marks - political/social ideologies overshadowing true teaching; leads to prejudice, oppression, violence; leaders' worldly ambition (Armstrong); gap between ideal (Nostra aetate) and lived experience.

rows.prompt: Describe one example of a religious initiative that works to overcome conflict between faiths.
rows.model_answer: Deir Mar Musa, the Community of St Moses the Ethiopian, was founded by Paolo Dall'Oglio, an Italian Jesuit priest, high on a cliff in the Syrian desert. The community prays, works and offers hospitality to all who come. Its aim is to encourage positive relationships between Muslims and Christians in a spirit of respect, love and reconciliation. Father Dall'Oglio says that 'everyone knows that we cannot continue to use religion as an excuse for violence of all kinds' and that 'we have to find a way to break through the infernal circle of fear that we feel, all of us.' The chapter says his words are a challenge for all people of faith in the twenty-first century. Another example is Pope John Paul II praying at Assisi in 1986 with Jews, Muslims, Hindus and Buddhists.
